content.title: About
content.content: Almonds are the edible seeds of the almond tree (Prunus dulcis), which is native to the Middle East and Central Asia and is now grown in many warm regions of the world. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Almonds are eaten raw, roasted, or blanched and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and almond milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almonds are related to peaches, plums, and cherries, and the almond itself is the seed inside the fruit's pit.
Sweet almonds are the ones eaten as food; bitter almonds contain compounds that are toxic when raw and are not sold as ordinary snacks.
Almond trees have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Almonds are used to make almond flour, almond butter, marzipan, and almond milk.
Almond blossoms appear in early spring, before the leaves.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds are one of the best food sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Almonds contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Almonds contribute plant protein and fiber, which support fullness.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Almonds contain more calcium than most other nuts.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almonds can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Almonds are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole almonds are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit. Bitter almonds should never be eaten raw.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Almonds can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, and baked goods, or ground into almond flour and almond butter. Soaking or blanching almonds softens them and makes the skins easy to remove. Unsalted or lightly salted almonds are a good option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store almonds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, since their oils can turn rancid. Discard almonds that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue beef, no sauce is a selection of beef cuts grilled or smoked with dry rubs, without any tomato‑based or other sauces. The product delivers a deep smoky aroma, a subtle sweet note, and a tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Barbecue culture originated in the southern United States, where beef was traditionally cooked over open flame.
Leaving out sauce lets the natural flavor of the meat and the spice blend shine through.
Only dry seasonings are used: salt, black pepper, paprika, garlic, and sometimes a touch of sugar.
Beef prepared without sauce retains more of its original nutrients, as sauces can add sugars and preservatives.
Cuts are often sliced against the grain to enhance tenderness.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support blood formation, immune function, and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Especially vitamin B12, which is important for nervous system health and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb and keto diets.

items.title: Contains creatine
items.content: Helps improve physical endurance and muscle strength.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Consume in moderation, particularly for individuals with elevated cholesterol.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Ensure the meat is fully cooked to eliminate harmful bacteria.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but possible for people with specific food allergies.

items.title: Sodium in the rub
items.content: Dry seasonings may contain salt; those monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Barbecue beef without sauce can be served as a main dish, thinly sliced for sandwiches, added to salads, pastas, or rice bowls. It pairs well with vegetable sides, fries, or fresh herb‑based dips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag where it remains good for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tangerine Juice 100% is a completely natural beverage made from fresh tangerines without added sugar, preservatives, or flavorings. It has a bright citrus aroma, a sweet‑tart taste, and is rich in vitamin C, B‑vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tangerines are often harvested in the early morning when their sugar content is at its peak.
The juice retains most nutrients thanks to rapid low‑temperature pasteurization.
In many countries, tangerine juice is a traditional breakfast drink served with bread or cereal.
It is frequently used in culinary applications as a base for marinades, sauces, and desserts.
The juice can be a source of the natural flavonoid hesperidin, which supports vascular health.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, supports collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for cell division and especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie beverage
items.content: One cup (250 ml) provides about 110 kcal, making it a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Provides antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High natural sugar content
items.content: Even without added sugar, the natural sugars can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tangerines.

items.title: Lack of fiber
items.content: Unlike whole fruit, the juice contains almost no dietary fiber, so it should be paired with fiber‑rich foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled, dilute with water, or use it in smoothies, cocktails, and marinades. To reduce acidity, a touch of honey or a pinch of salt can be added.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Freezing may alter texture but preserves nutrients.

content.title: About
content.content: Watermelon (Citrullus lanatus) is a large, refreshing fruit native to Africa, with a thick green rind and sweet, juicy red or pink flesh. It contains a lot of water and has a crisp, sweet flavor. Watermelon is eaten fresh in slices and cubes, blended into juices and smoothies, and used in salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Watermelon is about 90 percent water.
Watermelons were cultivated in Africa for thousands of years before spreading around the world.
Botanically, watermelon is a fruit called a pepo, related to cucumbers, pumpkins, and melons.
Its red color comes from lycopene, the same pigment found in tomatoes.
The seeds, rind, and flesh are all edible, and the rind is sometimes pickled.

items.title: Very hydrating
items.content: Watermelon is mostly water, making it refreshing in hot weather.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is an antioxidant pigment that helps protect cells against oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and vitamin A
items.content: These vitamins support the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains citrulline
items.content: Watermelon is a natural source of citrulline, an amino acid that is being studied.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Watermelon is low in calories for its volume.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Watermelon contains natural sugars, so portions matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Eating a lot of watermelon may cause bloating or loose stools in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people, especially those allergic to ragweed pollen, may experience itching or tingling in the mouth.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Wash the rind before cutting, because bacteria on the outside can be carried inward by the knife. Refrigerate cut watermelon.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Watermelon can be sliced or cubed and eaten fresh, blended into juices and smoothies, frozen into sorbets, or added to salads with feta, mint, or lime. The rind can be pickled or cooked. Chill it before serving for the best refreshing taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Whole watermelon can be kept at room temperature for a week or two and refrigerated once cut. Store cut watermelon in an airtight container in the refrigerator and eat it within three to five days. Discard watermelon that smells sour or has a slimy texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled zucchini are whole or sliced zucchini preserved in a brine of vinegar, spices, and sometimes sugar. They have a characteristic sweet‑sour flavor, a crisp texture, and retain most of the nutrients of fresh vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Zucchini belong to the cucurbit family and are a low‑calorie vegetable.
Pickling allows zucchini to be stored for several months without loss of taste.
Traditional brines include dill, garlic, mustard seeds, and chili pepper for aroma.
In some cuisines zucchini are pickled together with carrots and radishes to create mixed vegetable jars.
The acidity of the brine helps preserve vitamin C, which would otherwise degrade quickly.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Zucchini provide very few calories, making them ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Pickled zucchini retain vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: They contain lutein and zeaxanthin, which help maintain eye health.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Fermentation during pickling can foster beneficial bacteria.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled vegetables often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to dill, garlic, or mustard used in the brine.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of pathogenic bacteria, so adhere to shelf‑life guidelines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled zucchini can be added to salads, sandwiches, snack platters, used as a side for meat or fish, or as a filling for rolls and sushi.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the jar of pickled zucchini in the refrigerator at 2 °C–5 °C. Once opened, consume within 2–3 weeks. Discard if an off‑odor or mold appears.
